Return only one complete, self-contained IEC 61131-3 Structured Text FUNCTION_BLOCK implementation, including all VAR sections and END_FUNCTION_BLOCK. Use the exact input/output/inout names, types, directions and behavior in the user task. Use FUNCTION_BLOCK (not PROGRAM) for every task in this benchmark. Necessary named TYPE definitions may precede the block. Keep helper state inside VAR; do not emit nested FUNCTION/METHOD/ACTION or workspace-inspection commentary. Use supported standard ST constructs and explicit type conversions. Avoid CODESYS reserved local identifiers s and r; use SHL/SHR functions for shifts. Return a single fenced st block, without explanatory prose outside ST comments. Do not inspect files or request tools. The user task remains verbatim; these are shared packaging/output requirements for both frameworks. Target CODESYS 3.5 ST. End IF/CASE/FOR/WHILE/REPEAT statements with semicolons. In a CODESYS DUT, the top-level END_STRUCT is directly followed by END_TYPE; do not insert a semicolon between them. Nested STRUCT field declarations keep their required separators. Use ELSIF for a flat conditional chain; preserve balanced END_IF for true nested conditionals. Declare every enum and helper variable. Do not use AT located declarations in this function block. RETURN is a bare statement; assign declared outputs before RETURN, never RETURN an expression. Preserve exact interface types including UINT, LTIME and VARIANT; do not narrow or replace them. Respect stated latching and scan behavior; do not add unstated edge-only triggers, resets or interlocks. Keep reasoning concise and emit only the implementation.
Before implementing, put a concise ENGINEERING_CONTRACT comment inside the ST block (up to 12 lines). For each output or state group state: activation, retention/hold, explicit reset/deactivation, same-scan priority, and units/boundaries. Cite PUB clause IDs where relevant. This is a reviewable design table, not a reasoning transcript. Use only the task's public requirements. Preserve output state when the task explicitly requires retention; do not assume a mutually exclusive state machine automatically shuts down earlier outputs. Do not invent resets, interlocks, edge triggers or operation priorities. Mark unspecified details as unspecified and implement a consistent interpretation. Check strict > versus >=, boundary scan timing, TIME milliseconds versus LTIME nanoseconds, zero/reset behavior, array slot versus stored identifier and simultaneous operations when applicable. Return the table as an ST comment followed by the complete implementation in the same single fenced ST block. Missing table is recorded as process compliance, not a functional scoring failure. Also emit a separate ST comment (* CONTRACT_RULES [...] *) containing a JSON list for any unconditional public Boolean output latch explicitly required by the task. Each supported rule has kind=hold_until_reset, output=<public BOOL output>, set_input=<public BOOL input>, reset_input=<public BOOL input or null>. Use [] when no such unconditional latch is specified. The checker executes these declarations on generated public-input traces; do not declare conditions the implementation does not satisfy. These checks supplement the task and do not change its scoring.
Target tools: CODESYS 3.5 native compilation; deterministic local scan interpreter; bounded LTL checking after functional success. Supported core: IF/ELSIF, nested CASE, FOR/WHILE/REPEAT, named or anonymous integer enums, declared STRUCT/ARRAY, TIME/LTIME, TON, R_TRIG/F_TRIG, bit selectors, SHL/SHR, explicit IEC conversions and exact generic TO_BOOL/integer/bit conversions. Prefer explicit source_TO_target conversions, especially for REAL. Declare helper types and functions before use; avoid external library helpers unless supplied by the task. Keep every original public interface type and field spelling. Tool limits never authorize changing the task interface. Do not replace LTIME with floating-point arithmetic or VARIANT with DINT. CODESYS STRING scalar indexing is zero-based and returns BYTE, not a one-character STRING. For ASCII text, iterate byte indices 0 through LEN(text)-1, or use MID(text,1,position) with one-based position to get a one-character STRING. Do not mix those indexing conventions. Whole STRUCT and ARRAY assignments copy values. Generic TO_LREAL accepts numeric/BOOL operands; TO_REAL rounds to IEEE binary32. R_TRIG/F_TRIG and TON keep state across calls. On same-scan state changes determine the final timer enable before calling the timer so a newly enabled output and its elapsed-time origin agree. When multiple command inputs are asserted, preserve the public operation contracts or explicitly report an unsupported combination through an existing error interface; do not silently drop commands through an arbitrary priority. Prefix helper local names with tmp_ or local_ to avoid collisions with standard functions and reserved words, including LEN, S and R. Never shadow a standard function that the block calls. RETURN terminates the entire current function-block invocation, including when nested in IF, CASE or a loop; it does not clear retained state. EXIT terminates only the innermost loop. Standard TON.Q uses elapsed >= PT and TON.ET saturates at PT. Determine whether a threshold is strict from its public wording; apply the supplied arithmetic only to the quoted condition and its stated time resolution. Do not add a scan of delay by reading a stale timer Q. For every task independently audit: reset/stop priority, state retention, first invocation versus later invocations, rising-edge memory, array lower bounds and ordinal positions, stored identifier versus slot, numeric width, and simultaneous operations as explicitly specified. A sequence counterexample contains its complete public prefix; replay it from the stated initialization, preserving state between scans. Fix the cause while retaining already correct paths. No task ID, reference program or private assertion is a design rule.

# Mechanical Arm Control - **Difficulty:** Hard (hard) ## Requirements Design a PLC program to control an automated mechanical arm that performs handling tasks on the production line. The mechanical arm has six basic actions: down, up, left, right, grip, and release. The operating modes of the mechanical arm include four types: manual, single step, single cycle, and continuous. Control requirements: 1. Manual mode: Allows the operator to control each action of the mechanical arm individually through the control panel, provided it is not yet in position. For example, pressing the down button (DownButton=1), if not at the down position (DownLimitSwitch=0), then move down (MoveDown=1); if at the down position (DownLimitSwitch=1), stop moving down. Releasing the down button also stops the movement down. 2. Single step mode: The mechanical arm automatically executes one action according to the preset program, and the operator needs to confirm after each action is completed to execute the next action. The initial position of the mechanical arm is at the top left. When the start button is pressed once, the mechanical arm executes the down command MoveDown, and stops after reaching the down position. When the start button is pressed again, the mechanical arm executes the grip command ActivateGrip, and stops after gripping. When the start button is pressed again, the mechanical arm executes the up command MoveUp, and stops after reaching the up position. When the start button is pressed, the mechanical arm executes the right command MoveRight, and stops after reaching the right position. When the start button is pressed, the mechanical arm executes the down command MoveDown, and stops after reaching the down position. When the start button is pressed, the mechanical arm executes the release command ActivateRelease, and stops after releasing. When the start button is pressed again, the mechanical arm executes the up command MoveUp, and stops after reaching the up position. When the start button is pressed again, the mechanical arm executes the left command MoveLeft, and stops after reaching the left position. Then starts the cycle again from the beginning 3. Single cycle mode: The mechanical arm automatically completes a full handling cycle, including all preset actions, and stops at the end of the cycle waiting for the operator's instruction. The initial position of the mechanical arm is at the top left, when the start button is pressed: The mechanical arm first moves down, then grips after reaching the down position, moves up after gripping, moves right after reaching the up position, moves down after reaching the right position, releases after reaching the down position, moves up after releasing, moves left after reaching the up position, and stops after reaching the left position. 4. Continuous mode: The initial position of the mechanical arm is at the top left, when the start button is pressed, the mechanical arm continuously executes the handling cycle of the single cycle mode. 5. The emergency stop function can stop all actions of the mechanical arm at any time. Use GripLimitSwitch and ReleaseLimitSwitch as the completion feedback for gripping and releasing respectively. The caller keeps the four mode-selection inputs mutually exclusive. ## Interface Definition | Direction | Variable/Field | Data Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Input | `ManualMode` | `BOOL` | Manual mode | | Input | `SingleStepMode` | `BOOL` | Single step mode | | Input | `SingleCycleMode` | `BOOL` | Single cycle mode | | Input | `ContinuousMode` | `BOOL` | Continuous mode | | Input | `EmergencyStop` | `BOOL` | Emergency stop signal
